title: Kindle the fire of meditation (1.13–1.14)
hook: fire hides in the wood until someone drills for it; the Upanishad says the divine hides in you the same way
tomorrow: how to sit: the body straight, the senses withdrawn

segments.voice: Yesterday: the swan, hamsa, circling the great wheel until it stops believing it stands apart from the one who turns it. Did you let the swan land once? Today, the Upanishad hands you a tool. Day four hundred twenty-four.

Before matches, before lighters, a Vedic priest made the sacred fire from two pieces of wood. A flat lower block, a pointed upper stick. He set the stick in a notch, wrapped a cord around it, and pulled, back and forth, back and forth, until the wood smoked and a coal glowed. The two sticks were called the arani. Every household fire in the old rites began that way, with friction and patience. Now hold that picture, because the Shvetashvatara is about to say that you are the wood.
screen: `TWO STICKS OF WOOD.` → `BACK AND FORTH, UNTIL IT SMOKES.` → `YOU ARE THE WOOD.`

segments.voice: Verse 1.13, in paraphrase: the form of fire hidden in its source isn't seen, and yet it isn't destroyed. It can be caught again from the wood by drilling. In the same way, the self is caught in the body by om. Then verse 1.14 builds the whole fire kit. Make your own body the lower stick, and the sacred syllable om the upper stick. By the practice of churning, which is meditation, you will see God, like fire hidden in the wood. The Sanskrit word for that drilling is related to churning, the same motion as churning butter out of milk. And the next verses keep going with it: like oil in sesame seeds, butter in cream, water in a dry riverbed, fire in the fire sticks, the self is found within by one who seeks it with truth and discipline. Notice what this picture says and what it doesn't. It doesn't say the fire is missing. It says the fire is already there, invisible, undamaged. What's missing is friction, repeated and patient. One pull of the cord does nothing. A hundred pulls, and there's smoke. That is a remarkably practical description of meditation for a text this old: not a lightning bolt from outside, but a steady back and forth, om and body, breath and attention, until something kindles. And it sets up tomorrow, where the Upanishad tells you how to sit while you do it.
screen: `THE FIRE HIDES, BUT ISN'T LOST.` · `BODY BELOW, OM ABOVE.` · `OIL IN SESAME, BUTTER IN CREAM.` · then, large: `CHURN, AND THE FIRE APPEARS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and feel the weight of your body, the lower stick. On each out-breath, let a long, quiet om sound inside you, or out loud if that's comfortable, the upper stick. Breath in, rest. Breath out, om. Don't look for sparks. Just keep the gentle back and forth going, the way the old priests kept the cord moving. If your attention wanders, that's one pull of the cord. Come back and pull again. The bell holds the time.
Arani, the fire-drilling sticks. The Shvetashvatara's picture of practice: the body as one stick, om as the other, and steady churning until the hidden fire shows.
Your line: the churning. Pick one thing you keep coming back to, a habit, a practice, a hard conversation, and treat today's small effort as one more pull of the cord. Day four hundred twenty-four.

screen: `DAY 424 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HOW TO SIT: THE BODY STRAIGHT, THE SENSES WITHDRAWN.`

howItsDone: In Vedic ritual the sacred fire is still kindled by drilling the arani fire sticks at some major rites, and many Hindus who meditate use om, silently or aloud, as the steady repetition the Upanishad describes.

match.prompt: the fire kit of 1.14: tap the pairs.

myth: the verse says the fire is missing until meditation creates it
1.13 says the fire hidden in the wood isn't seen, but isn't destroyed. it is already there.
the Upanishad compares the hidden self to oil in sesame seeds
and butter in cream, water in a dry riverbed, fire in the fire sticks (1.15).
the arani were two pieces of wood used to make the sacred fire
a lower block and an upper drill, worked back and forth.

fork.setup: you've drilled the fire sticks a dozen times and seen no smoke. what does the Upanishad's picture suggest?
options: the wood has no fire in it.
keep churning: the fire is there, it takes repeated friction.
throw the sticks away and wait for lightning.
fork.reveal: the verses insist the fire is hidden, not absent. it is caught by drilling, by the practice of churning, which the text calls meditation.

original.note: Sanskrit araṇi: the fire-drilling sticks of Vedic ritual. in 1.14 the body is the lower one, om the upper.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'kindle the fire' is a nice way of saying 'try harder'.
what it means: the divine is already present within, like fire in wood, and repeated meditation brings it into view.
what a scholar hears: the image borrows the arani of the Vedic fire rite and turns ritual into inner practice, the same move the Upanishads make again and again.

sources.ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.13–1.14 (fire hidden in the wood; body and om as fire sticks)
Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.15–1.16 (oil in sesame, butter in cream, water in springs, fire in the fire sticks)

notes: 'Churning' renders dhyana-nirmathana (the drilling/churning of meditation) in 1.14; confirm wording.
'Water in a dry riverbed' renders srotas (springs/streams) in 1.15; Müller has 'water in (dry) river-beds'. Please check.
Use of arani in present-day shrauta rites is stated generally ('at some major rites'); confirm.
